tutorials.title: Baking Soda and Vinegar
tutorials.body: When you pour vinegar onto baking soda, the acid in the vinegar reacts with the base in the baking soda and makes a brand-new gas called carbon dioxide. That gas needs somewhere to go, so it pushes up and out as the foamy bubbles you see erupting in a homemade volcano. It is a chemical change, because the fizzing leaves behind something different from what you started with. The same gas is what makes bread and cake rise and puff up in the oven.

tutorials.title: Solubility and Temperature
tutorials.body: Solubility is how much of a substance can dissolve in a liquid, and for most solids it goes up when the liquid is warmer. Heat makes the liquid's particles move faster and bump the solid apart more eagerly, so more of it can squeeze in. That is why you can stir a heap of sugar into hot tea but the same amount just sinks and sits in iced tea. Let the sweet hot tea cool slowly and some sugar may even creep back out as tiny crystals.

tutorials.title: Sublimation
tutorials.body: Sublimation is the unusual trick where a solid turns straight into a gas without ever becoming a liquid in between. It happens because the particles gain enough energy to break free all at once instead of loosening into a puddle first. The clearest example is dry ice, the frozen form of carbon dioxide, which never melts into a liquid but instead fogs away as a chilly gas. The same thing slowly happens to ice cubes left forgotten in the freezer, which shrink over time even though they never get wet.

tutorials.title: Incomplete Dominance
tutorials.body: In incomplete dominance, neither allele fully masks the other, so the heterozygote shows a blended in-between trait rather than one parent's. Classic example: a red snapdragon crossed with a white one gives pink flowers, because half the usual red pigment is made. A Punnett square of two pinks (Rr x Rr) predicts 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so here the genotype ratio and the phenotype ratio match exactly.

triggers: how is codominance different from incomplete dominance
tutorials.title: Codominance
tutorials.body: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed at the same time, so the heterozygote shows both traits side by side rather than a blend. A roan cow with a red-and-white speckled coat is a good example: it has both pure red hairs and pure white hairs, not pink ones. This is different from incomplete dominance, where the two alleles average into a single new appearance like pink.

tutorials.title: Multiple Alleles (ABO Blood Type)
tutorials.body: Some genes have more than two possible alleles in the population, even though any one person still carries only two. The ABO blood gene has three alleles: A and B are codominant with each other, while O is recessive to both. So a parent with IA IB blood is type AB, and a child who inherits one O allele from each parent is type O even if grandparents were A and B.

tutorials.title: Dihybrid Cross
tutorials.body: A dihybrid cross tracks two different traits at the same time, like seed shape and seed color in peas. Each parent can pass four allele combinations, so the Punnett square has sixteen boxes instead of four. When you cross two parents heterozygous for both traits, the classic phenotype ratio that comes out is nine showing both dominant traits, three and three showing one dominant each, and one showing both recessive.

tutorials.title: Test Cross
tutorials.body: A test cross reveals whether an organism showing a dominant trait is homozygous or heterozygous, since both look identical on the outside. You cross the mystery individual with a homozygous recessive partner and watch the offspring. If any offspring show the recessive trait, the mystery parent must have carried a hidden recessive allele; if all offspring show the dominant trait, it was almost certainly homozygous dominant.

tutorials.title: Genetic Carrier
tutorials.body: A carrier is someone who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the trait because their other allele is dominant. They are healthy themselves yet can pass the recessive allele to their children. If two carriers have a child, a Punnett square predicts a one-in-four chance the child inherits both recessive copies and shows the trait, which is how conditions like cystic fibrosis can appear in families with no visible history.

tutorials.title: Sex-Linked Inheritance
tutorials.body: Sex-linked genes sit on the X or Y chromosome, so they are inherited along with biological sex. Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on it, such as the one for red-green color blindness, shows up with no second copy to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes and usually need both copies to be recessive, which is why X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males.

tutorials.title: Polygenic Traits
tutorials.body: A polygenic trait is controlled by many genes acting together, so instead of a few distinct categories you get a smooth range of outcomes. Human height and skin color work this way, which is why a class of people forms a bell-shaped spread rather than just tall or short. A single Punnett square cannot capture this, because each gene adds a small amount to the total effect.

tutorials.title: Pleiotropy
tutorials.body: Pleiotropy is when a single gene affects several seemingly unrelated traits at once. The same gene change can ripple into many body systems because its protein is used in more than one place. In sickle cell disease, for example, one altered gene changes the shape of red blood cells, which in turn affects oxygen delivery, pain, organ function, and even resistance to malaria.

tutorials.title: Epistasis
tutorials.body: Epistasis is when one gene masks or overrides the effect of a completely different gene. A common example is coat color in Labrador retrievers: one gene decides whether the pigment is black or brown, but a second gene can switch pigment off entirely and produce a yellow lab regardless of what the first gene says. So a dog can carry black-coat alleles yet still be yellow because the masking gene won out.

tutorials.title: The 3:1 Monohybrid Ratio
tutorials.body: When you cross two heterozygotes for one trait, such as Bb crossed with Bb, the four-box Punnett square gives one BB, two Bb, and one bb. Because both BB and Bb show the dominant trait, three of the four boxes look dominant and only one looks recessive, producing the famous 3:1 phenotype ratio. The genotype ratio underneath is actually 1:2:1, which is hidden because the heterozygotes look just like the dominant homozygotes.

tutorials.title: Linkage and Crossing Over
tutorials.body: Genes that sit close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited as a package, which is called linkage, so they break the usual independent-assortment rules behind Punnett squares. During the formation of egg and sperm cells, matching chromosomes can swap matching segments in a process called crossing over, which shuffles alleles and can separate even linked genes. The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the less often crossing over splits them apart.

tutorials.title: Genotype vs. Phenotype
tutorials.body: The genotype is the actual set of alleles an organism carries, while the phenotype is the trait you can observe, such as eye color or height. The same phenotype can come from different genotypes, because a dominant trait shows up whether you have one or two dominant alleles. That is exactly why a Punnett square's genotype ratio of 1:2:1 collapses into a 3:1 phenotype ratio, and why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

tutorials.title: Seafloor Spreading
tutorials.body: At mid-ocean ridges, two plates pull apart and hot rock rises from the mantle to fill the gap, cooling into fresh seafloor that pushes the older crust outward on both sides. This means the ocean floor is youngest right at the ridge and gets steadily older the farther away you look. Picture a conveyor belt: new material is added in the middle and carried sideways, slowly widening the ocean over millions of years. This is part of why the Atlantic Ocean is still getting a little wider every year.

tutorials.title: Subduction Zones
tutorials.body: Where two plates collide and one is denser, the heavier plate bends and sinks beneath the lighter one back down into the mantle. As the sinking slab heats up, it releases water that lowers the melting point of the rock above it, feeding chains of volcanoes near the boundary. Think of pushing one edge of a floating rug under another until it slips below the surface. This is why volcanoes and deep ocean trenches often line up along the same coastlines.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why oceanic crust subducts under continental crust and not the other way around.

tutorials.title: Transform Faults
tutorials.body: A transform fault is a boundary where two plates grind horizontally past each other instead of pulling apart or colliding, so no crust is created or destroyed. The rough surfaces snag and build up strain until they suddenly slip, which is what produces earthquakes there. It is like two bricks sliding past one another with their gritty faces catching, then jerking free. The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example separating two plates moving in opposite directions.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why transform faults usually don't make volcanoes.

tutorials.title: Convergent Boundaries
tutorials.body: A convergent boundary is where two plates move toward each other, and what happens depends on what kinds of crust meet. Ocean-meets-ocean or ocean-meets-continent leads to subduction and volcanic arcs, while continent-meets-continent crumples both edges upward because neither is dense enough to sink. The result can be towering mountain ranges, deep trenches, or strings of volcanoes. It is like two cars in a head-on collision: the metal has nowhere to go but up and outward.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me which kind of convergent boundary built the Himalayas.

tutorials.title: Divergent Boundaries
tutorials.body: A divergent boundary is where two plates move away from each other, letting hot mantle rock rise and create brand-new crust in the gap. Under the ocean this builds mid-ocean ridges, and on land it forms rift valleys where the ground stretches, thins, and drops down between cracks. Imagine slowly pulling apart a stretched piece of taffy until the middle thins and tears. East Africa is being torn apart this way right now and may eventually split off into a new sea.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me whether a continent can rip apart into two.

tutorials.title: Ridge Push and Slab Pull
tutorials.body: Plates don't just drift randomly; two forces do most of the pushing and pulling. Ridge push happens because the elevated, hot rock at a mid-ocean ridge slides downhill and shoves the plate away, while slab pull happens when a cold, dense subducting slab sinks and drags the rest of the plate behind it like a tablecloth slipping off a table. Slab pull is generally considered the stronger of the two. Underlying mantle convection helps, but these edge forces dominate the motion of a plate.

tutorials.title: Hotspots and Mantle Plumes
tutorials.body: A hotspot is a fixed column of unusually hot rock rising from deep in the mantle that melts through the plate above it, creating volcanoes far from any plate boundary. Because the plume stays roughly in place while the plate slides over it, it punches out a trail of volcanoes, with the oldest ones carried farthest away and the active one sitting over the plume now. Think of holding a candle under a sheet of paper you slowly drag across it, leaving a line of scorch marks. The Hawaiian island chain formed exactly this way.

tutorials.title: The Wadati-Benioff Zone
tutorials.body: A Wadati-Benioff zone is the sloping band of earthquakes that traces a subducting slab as it dives deeper into the mantle. The quakes get progressively deeper the farther you move inland from the trench, mapping out the angle and path of the descending plate even though we can't see it directly. It is like dropping a marked stick into murky water and tracking it only by the bubbles rising along its length. These deep quake patterns gave early scientists some of the first clear proof that whole slabs really sink into the mantle.

tutorials.title: Isostasy
tutorials.body: Isostasy is the idea that the rigid plates float on the denser, slowly flowing mantle beneath them, finding a balance like ice cubes bobbing in water. Thicker or lighter crust rides higher and also pushes a deeper root down below, which is why tall mountain ranges have thick crustal roots underneath them. When a heavy ice sheet melts away, the land it was pressing down slowly rebounds upward over thousands of years. Parts of Scandinavia and Canada are still rising today for exactly that reason.

tutorials.title: Accretionary Wedge
tutorials.body: An accretionary wedge is a pile of seafloor sediment and rock that gets scraped off a subducting plate and plastered onto the edge of the overriding plate. As the lower plate dives down, the soft material on top is shaved off and stacked into a wedge-shaped, folded heap near the trench. Picture a snowplow pushing snow into a growing ridge in front of its blade. Over time these wedges can grow large enough to become dry land or even contribute to building coastal mountains.

tutorials.title: Triple Junctions
tutorials.body: A triple junction is a point where three tectonic plate boundaries meet, so three plates share a single corner. The boundaries can be any mix of ridges, trenches, and transform faults, and some combinations are stable and stay put while others slowly migrate over time. Think of the spot where three slices of a pie all come to a point in the center. The Afar region in East Africa sits near such a junction, where rifting in several directions is pulling the crust apart at once.

tutorials.title: The Wilson Cycle
tutorials.body: The Wilson cycle describes the long-term life story of an ocean basin: continents rift apart, a new ocean opens and widens through seafloor spreading, then subduction begins, the ocean closes, and finally the continents collide to raise mountains. The cycle can take hundreds of millions of years to run its course before starting over. It is like a slow breath in and out, with oceans being born, growing, and disappearing again. The Atlantic is currently in its opening stage while remnants of older closed oceans are recorded inside mountain belts like the Appalachians.

tutorials.title: Sonic Boom
tutorials.body: A sonic boom is the loud crack you hear when an object travels faster than the speed of sound. The object outruns its own pressure waves, so those waves pile up into a single sharp shock front shaped like a cone trailing behind it. When that cone sweeps over your ears, all the built-up pressure arrives at once as a bang. A supersonic jet doesn't boom only when it 'breaks the barrier' — it drags the boom along the ground the whole time it's flying that fast.

tutorials.title: Mach Number and the Sound Barrier
tutorials.body: The Mach number is an object's speed divided by the local speed of sound, so Mach 1 means moving exactly as fast as sound travels in that air. The 'sound barrier' isn't a wall — it's the sharp rise in air resistance that happens as an aircraft approaches Mach 1, because the air can't get out of the way fast enough and pressure waves stack up in front. Above Mach 1 the craft is supersonic and outruns its own sound. Because the speed of sound drops in colder, thinner high-altitude air, the same true speed can be a higher Mach number up high than at sea level.

tutorials.title: Why Decibels Are Logarithmic
tutorials.body: Human hearing spans an enormous range of sound intensities, so loudness is measured on the decibel scale, which is logarithmic rather than linear. Each increase of about ten decibels represents roughly ten times more sound intensity, even though our ears perceive it as only 'about twice as loud.' That's why a whisper and a jet engine can be described with numbers that look close together but differ by trillions in actual energy. It also means two identical sound sources together are only about three decibels louder than one, not double the decibel number.

tutorials.title: Beat Frequency
tutorials.body: When two sounds of slightly different frequencies play together, they drift in and out of step, alternately reinforcing and cancelling each other. The result is a slow throbbing in loudness called a beat, and the number of throbs per second equals the difference between the two frequencies. Musicians use this to tune instruments: as two strings get closer in pitch, the beats slow down, and when the wobble disappears entirely the notes match. You can hear it as a 'wah-wah-wah' pulse when two people hum almost-but-not-quite the same note.

tutorials.title: Sound Diffraction
tutorials.body: Diffraction is the way waves bend around edges and spread out after passing through gaps, and sound does it readily because its wavelengths are large — often comparable to the size of everyday doorways and walls. That bending is why you can hear someone talking in the next room even when you can't see them around the corner. Low, long-wavelength sounds like bass diffract more than high, short-wavelength sounds, which is part of why you mainly hear the thumping bass from a party down the street while the crisp treble is lost.

tutorials.title: Refraction of Sound Through Air Layers
tutorials.body: Sound travels faster in warmer air, so when air temperature changes with height, sound waves bend toward the cooler, slower layers. On a sunny day the ground is hot and the air above is cooler, so sound bends upward and away from a listener, making distant sounds fade quickly. At night the ground cools and a warm layer sits above, so sound bends back down toward the ground and carries much farther. That's why a train horn or distant voices can sound surprisingly clear across a lake on a calm evening.

tutorials.title: Acoustic Impedance
tutorials.body: Acoustic impedance describes how much a material resists being set into vibration by a sound wave, and it depends on the material's density and the speed of sound within it. When a sound wave hits a boundary between two materials with very different impedances, most of the energy reflects instead of crossing over. That's why sound made in air mostly bounces off a water surface rather than entering it, and why ultrasound machines use a gel to bridge the impedance gap between the probe and your skin so the sound can get inside.

tutorials.title: Reverberation
tutorials.body: Reverberation is the lingering wash of sound that remains after a source stops, made of countless reflections bouncing off walls, floors, and ceilings and arriving at your ears slightly delayed. Unlike a distinct echo, these reflections blur together into a smooth tail because each surface sends sound back many times. Hard, bare rooms reverberate a lot and sound boomy, while curtains, carpet, and furniture absorb the energy and deaden it. Concert halls are tuned for just enough reverberation to make music feel rich without smearing the notes together.

tutorials.title: Moving Source vs Moving Observer
tutorials.body: The Doppler effect for sound is not perfectly symmetric: it matters whether the source is moving or the listener is, because sound travels through air, which acts as a fixed reference medium. A moving source bunches up the actual wave crests in front of it, while a moving listener simply runs into or away from crests faster. At everyday speeds the two cases give almost the same pitch shift, but the underlying math differs slightly. This is unlike the Doppler effect for light, where only the relative motion matters because light needs no medium.

tutorials.title: Doppler Radar
tutorials.body: Doppler radar bounces radio waves off a moving target and measures how the reflected wave's frequency has shifted, using that shift to calculate the target's speed toward or away from the device. A police speed gun does this to a passing car, while weather radar uses it to see how fast rain and wind are moving inside a storm, revealing rotation that can signal a tornado. Because it relies on the Doppler shift, it measures only the part of the motion along the radar beam, so a car crossing sideways would barely register.

tutorials.title: Relativistic Doppler Effect
tutorials.body: For light from very fast-moving sources, the ordinary Doppler shift is modified by special relativity, because the source's clock runs slow from the observer's point of view. This adds an extra time-dilation factor on top of the usual frequency change, and it even produces a transverse Doppler shift — a redshift you see when the source moves straight across your line of sight, where classical theory predicts no shift at all. Astronomers must use these relativistic formulas when measuring the speeds of distant galaxies and fast jets of matter near black holes.

tutorials.title: What Sets the Speed of Sound in a Material
tutorials.body: The speed of sound in a material depends on two competing properties: its stiffness, which speeds sound up, and its density, which slows it down. Solids like steel are extremely stiff, so even though they are dense, sound races through them many times faster than through air. This is why you can hear a distant train sooner by pressing your ear to the rail than by listening through the air. It also explains why sound is faster in water than in air but slower in lead than in aluminum, since stiffness usually wins out over density.

tutorials.title: Active Noise Cancellation
tutorials.body: Active noise-cancelling headphones use a tiny microphone to listen to incoming sound, then play back a matching wave that is exactly inverted — its peaks line up with the noise's troughs. When the two waves meet, they undergo destructive interference and largely cancel, leaving near silence. This works best on steady low-frequency drones like an airplane engine, because the headphones can predict and invert that smooth wave; sudden, high-pitched sounds are too quick and irregular to cancel cleanly. It's the same wave-cancelling idea as beats, but aimed at erasing sound rather than making it pulse.

tutorials.title: Induced Fit vs Lock-and-Key
tutorials.body: The old lock-and-key idea pictured an enzyme's active site as a rigid slot the substrate slips into. The induced-fit model is closer to reality: the active site is flexible and reshapes itself slightly around the substrate once it arrives, gripping it and straining its bonds toward the reaction. It is less like a stiff lock and more like a hand closing around a ball it has just caught.

tutorials.title: Cofactors and Coenzymes
tutorials.body: Many enzymes can't work alone and need a non-protein helper called a cofactor. Cofactors that are metal ions (like zinc or iron) lock into the enzyme, while organic helpers are called coenzymes, several of which your body builds from vitamins. The bare protein is the apoenzyme; add its cofactor and you get the active holoenzyme. This is one reason vitamin deficiencies can stall whole chunks of your metabolism.

tutorials.title: Competitive Inhibition
tutorials.body: A competitive inhibitor is a molecule shaped enough like the real substrate to slot into the active site, where it just sits and blocks the substrate from binding. Because it competes for the same spot, flooding the cell with more substrate can outcompete it and restore the reaction. Many drugs work this way, jamming an enzyme's active site so its normal job slows down.

tutorials.title: Allosteric Regulation
tutorials.body: Some enzymes have a second binding spot away from the active site called an allosteric site. When a regulator molecule docks there, it bends the whole protein into a different shape, turning the active site on or off without touching it directly. This lets cells dial enzymes up or down on the fly, like a thermostat that responds to how much product has already piled up.

tutorials.title: Feedback Inhibition
tutorials.body: In a chain of reactions where each enzyme hands its product to the next, the final product often loops back and switches off the first enzyme in the line. That way the cell stops spending raw materials the moment it has made enough, then resumes when stocks run low. It is the same logic as a factory that pauses the assembly line once the warehouse is full.

tutorials.title: Temperature, pH, and Denaturation
tutorials.body: Every enzyme has a sweet spot of temperature and pH where its precise folded shape works best. Push the heat or acidity too far and the protein unravels, a permanent change called denaturation that wrecks the active site. It is exactly what happens when you fry an egg: the heat denatures its proteins, and they never go back to clear and runny.

tutorials.title: Glycolysis
tutorials.body: Glycolysis is the opening act of breaking down sugar: a chain of enzymes splits one glucose into two smaller pyruvate molecules right in the cell's cytoplasm. It spends a little energy up front to gain more back, netting a small amount of ATP plus electron carriers for later stages. Crucially it needs no oxygen, which is why it is the oldest and most universal energy trick in life.

tutorials.title: The Citric Acid Cycle
tutorials.body: Also called the Krebs cycle, this is a loop of reactions in the mitochondria that finishes pulling apart the carbons from food. Each turn strips off carbon dioxide you breathe out and loads up electron carriers that feed the next stage. Think of it as the spinning gear that doesn't make much energy directly but charges up the batteries the cell will cash in afterward.

tutorials.title: The Electron Transport Chain
tutorials.body: This is where cells make the bulk of their ATP. Electron carriers charged up earlier dump their electrons into a row of proteins in the mitochondrial membrane, and the energy released pumps protons to one side. Those protons then rush back through a turbine-like enzyme that spins to crank out ATP, a process called chemiosmosis. Oxygen sits at the very end to grab the spent electrons, which is the whole reason you need to breathe.

tutorials.title: ATP Synthase
tutorials.body: ATP synthase is a tiny molecular motor embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. Protons crowded on one side flow back through it like water through a dam, physically spinning part of the enzyme. That rotation snaps a phosphate onto ADP to build ATP, the cell's rechargeable energy battery. It is one of the few cases in biology where you can literally call a protein a spinning turbine.

tutorials.title: Fermentation
tutorials.body: When oxygen runs short, cells can't finish the usual energy chain, so they fall back on fermentation to keep glycolysis running. In your muscles, hard sprinting builds up lactic acid this way, contributing to that burning, tired feeling. Yeast does a different version, turning sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is exactly how bread rises and beer brews.

tutorials.title: Anabolism vs Catabolism
tutorials.body: Your metabolism runs two opposite directions at once. Catabolism breaks big molecules down into smaller ones and releases energy, like digesting a meal into usable fuel. Anabolism spends that energy to build big molecules up, like knitting amino acids into the muscle you grow after a workout. Tearing down and building up are constantly traded off depending on whether you've just eaten or are running on reserves.

tutorials.title: Gluconeogenesis
tutorials.body: When you haven't eaten and blood sugar dips, your liver builds fresh glucose from non-sugar sources like amino acids and lactate. It is roughly glycolysis run in reverse, but it uses a few different enzymes to push past the steps that normally only flow one way. This is what keeps your brain, a glucose hog, fueled through an overnight fast or a long stretch without food.

tutorials.title: Deposition (Gas to Solid)
tutorials.body: Deposition is when a gas turns straight into a solid without ever passing through the liquid stage, the exact reverse of sublimation. The vapor particles lose energy and lock into a solid arrangement all at once instead of first puddling into a liquid. Frost on a cold window or on the grass is the classic example: water vapor in the air freezes directly onto the chilly surface as delicate ice crystals.

tutorials.title: The Triple Point
tutorials.body: The triple point is the single, exact combination of temperature and pressure where a substance can exist as solid, liquid, and gas all at the same time, in balance. At that precise point ice, water, and steam can sit together in the same container without any one of them winning out. It is so reliable and reproducible that scientists long used water's triple point to help define the temperature scale itself.

tutorials.title: Supercritical Fluids
tutorials.body: Push a substance past its critical point, a special temperature and pressure, and the difference between liquid and gas simply disappears, leaving a single state called a supercritical fluid. It can flow and fill a container like a gas but dissolve things like a liquid, blurring the usual boundary. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used industrially to decaffeinate coffee beans, since it soaks out the caffeine but leaves no harmful residue behind.

tutorials.title: Plasma: The Fourth State of Matter
tutorials.body: Heat a gas hot enough, or zap it with strong energy, and electrons get torn away from their atoms, leaving a glowing soup of charged particles called plasma. Because it is full of free charges, plasma conducts electricity and bends to magnetic fields in ways an ordinary gas cannot. You meet it every day in lightning, neon signs, and the flickering glow of the Sun, which is itself an enormous ball of plasma.

tutorials.title: Bose-Einstein Condensate
tutorials.body: A Bose-Einstein condensate is an exotic state that forms when certain atoms are cooled to a whisker above absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible. At that point the atoms slow almost to a standstill and merge into one shared quantum blob, all behaving as a single entity rather than as separate particles. It is the opposite extreme from plasma: where plasma is matter at scorching energy, this is matter at the very bottom of the cold.

tutorials.title: Surface Tension
tutorials.body: Inside a liquid every molecule is pulled in all directions by its neighbors, but at the surface there are no neighbors above, so those molecules pull sideways and inward, forming a kind of stretchy skin. This is why water beads up into round droplets and why a gently placed paper clip or a water strider can rest on the surface without sinking. It also pulls small drops into the most compact shape possible, a sphere.

tutorials.title: Viscosity
tutorials.body: Viscosity is a liquid's resistance to flowing, set by how strongly its particles cling to and drag past one another. Thick, sticky liquids like honey or syrup have high viscosity and ooze slowly, while thin liquids like water have low viscosity and pour fast. Warming a liquid usually lowers its viscosity, which is why honey runs much more easily after you heat it.

tutorials.title: Boiling Point and Pressure
tutorials.body: A liquid boils when its escaping vapor pushes hard enough to match the air pressure pressing down on it, so lower air pressure lets it boil at a lower temperature. On a high mountain the thinner air means water boils well below its sea-level temperature, so cooking takes longer because the water is cooler. A pressure cooker does the opposite: it traps steam to raise the pressure, letting water get hotter than usual and cook food faster.

tutorials.title: Supercooling
tutorials.body: Supercooling is when a very pure, undisturbed liquid is chilled below its normal freezing point yet stays liquid, because it has no speck or jolt to trigger the first crystals. Freezing usually needs a starting point such as a dust grain or a scratch, and without one the molecules cannot get organized. A bottle of very clean water can sometimes be cooled below freezing and then snap into ice the instant you tap it or drop in a single crystal.
